lessons.title: JSX and pure components
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of deterministic component rendering in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of deterministic component rendering.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: React calls a component function to obtain a JSX description, compares it with the previous description, and applies minimal DOM changes. Rendering must remain a pure calculation: same props, same description, with no external writes during the call. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: deterministic component rendering is like a building-block set where each piece receives measurements and always produces the same shape. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

JSX accepts JavaScript expressions inside braces but requires valid elements and attributes; className and htmlFor correspond to React DOM properties. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

A component isolates one visual responsibility and uses a domain name; Price explains intent better than a generic renderThing function. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

The render body performs no imperative fetch, localStorage write, or global mutation because repeated development renders would then produce different results. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.

lessons.title: Events and data flow
prerequisites: Know how to open the L’ecomax project in VS Code and use its integrated terminal.
Have read the previous lesson and be able to explain the role of raising user intent in your own words.
objectives: Build an accurate mental model of raising user intent.
Write and run a minimal example before integrating it into a real feature.
Recognize failure states, read their symptoms, and apply a verifiable correction.

blocks.text: Data moves down through props and intent moves up through callbacks. The button component knows the click and identifier, but the parent that owns the cart decides how that intent changes the application. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: raising user intent is like a building-block set where each piece receives measurements and always produces the same shape. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

onClick receives a function to call later; writing onClick={onAdd(productId)} executes during render and passes its result instead of a callback. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

handleClick names the local event while onAdd names the domain intent sent to the parent; the distinction clarifies responsibility. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

disabled truly prevents keyboard and pointer activation; text explains the state instead of relying only on gray color. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.
